documents.unit: Rutgers Office of Information Technology (all campuses)
documents.title: Guidance on the use of AI at Rutgers
documents.stance_why: The page says guidance 'will typically vary depending on the discipline, course, and/or instructor' and tells students to follow 'their program and instructors' guidance', so the decision is delegated. It adds a fallback that AI 'should not be considered permissible for coursework unless clearly stated or communicated by instructors', but sets no university-wide permit or ban beyond that.
documents.summary: Short OIT guidance page for all Rutgers campuses. It directs users to Rutgers-approved AI tools, leaves academic AI rules to instructors with a default of not permissible unless stated, and covers data protection, verification of output, procurement, and relevant policies.

units.why: The sentence says 'only Rutgers-approved AI tools should be used' and gives the reason 'to protect university data', so it is a vetted-tool preference (P50) addressed to everyone doing university work.
units.anchor: only Rutgers-approved AI tools should be used at the university

units.why: States that approved versions of the tools do not train models on user data; a factual privacy assurance, so informs, and P50 (vetted tools protect data) is the place a reader would look.
units.anchor: your data will not be used to train the models underlying the tools

units.why: OIT says it 'provides access to generative AI tools with protections'; the university supplies sanctioned licensed tools, which is P17. P50 was considered but the point of this sentence is provision.
units.anchor: provides access to generative AI tools with protections for use in university work
units.fit_note: Provision is for university work generally, not a course-specific tool.

units.why: The page says academic-setting guidance 'will typically vary depending on the discipline, course, and/or instructor', so the university sets no single rule and hands the decision to instructors (P04).
units.anchor: guidance on the appropriate use of AI tools in academic settings will typically vary

units.why: Faculty 'should consider providing guidance to students', a soft recommendation that instructors communicate AI expectations; closest to P09 although it is only 'consider'.
units.anchor: Faculty should consider providing guidance to students on the use of AI
units.fit_note: Only 'should consider', not a mandatory syllabus statement.

units.why: Students 'are encouraged to review course materials and speak with their instructors' to learn expectations, i.e. ask before using AI, so P10.
units.anchor: students are encouraged to review course materials and speak with their instructors

units.why: Sets the fallback: AI 'should not be considered permissible for coursework unless clearly stated or communicated by instructors'; a restrictive default when instructors are silent, P06.
units.anchor: should not be considered permissible for coursework unless clearly stated or communicated by instructors
units.frag_start: Though AI tools are widely available

units.why: 'Students are responsible for understanding and abiding by their program and instructors' guidance' puts the burden of knowing the rules on students; P29 fits partly since it concerns compliance, not ownership of work.
units.anchor: Students are responsible for understanding and abiding by their program and instructors
units.frag_end: rules on the use of AI
units.fit_note: Responsibility is for knowing and following rules, not for owning submitted work.

units.why: Quotes the Academic Integrity Policy requirement that coursework be 'created without the aid of impermissible technologies'; ties AI use to the integrity policy, so P36 (unauthorized use as misconduct).
units.anchor: coursework be “the student’s own and created without the aid of impermissible technologies
units.frag_start: the principles of academic integrity require
units.fit_note: The text never says 'misconduct' for AI explicitly; the link is through 'impermissible technologies'.

units.why: Warns that confidential information and PHI 'may not be appropriate for use in AI applications', a data-protection rule, P50.
units.anchor: may not be appropriate for use in AI applications and systems

units.why: Points readers to the data classification chart and Information Classification Policy 70.1.2, binding AI use to existing university policy, so P77.
units.anchor: Information Classification Policy 70.1.2
units.frag_start: this data classification chart for AI tools

units.why: 'Always review and verify AI content and outputs' is a direct verify-output rule (P31).
units.anchor: Always review and verify AI content and outputs.

units.why: States AI tools can produce biased and inaccurate information and uncredited copyrighted content, a risk statement supporting verification; closest P31.
units.anchor: AI tools can produce biased and inaccurate information
units.fit_note: Also mentions bias and uncredited copyrighted content (P53, P52).

units.why: 'You are responsible for ensuring the accuracy and appropriateness of AI-generated content' makes the user accountable for the output they use, P29.
units.anchor: You are responsible for ensuring the accuracy and appropriateness of AI-generated content
units.fit_note: Accountability for accuracy of AI content, rather than ownership of submissions.

units.why: Purchases of AI applications 'must follow the same security processes and risk assessments'; an institutional procurement rule, nearest P65 (review of AI vendors).
units.anchor: you must follow the same security processes and risk assessments
units.frag_start: If you are considering the purchase
units.fit_note: Covers procurement review, not vendor data-sharing limits.

units.why: Lists the Academic Integrity, Information Classification and Acceptable Use policies as 'particularly relevant for the use of AI', directing AI use under existing policies, P77.
units.anchor: particularly relevant for the use of AI at Rutgers

documents.unit: OTEAR (Office of Teaching Evaluation and Assessment Research)
documents.title: AI in Education - OTEAR Rutgers
documents.date_or_term: current (copyright 2026); page states it is archived and no longer maintained
tiers: not permitted in any stages of writing
only to brainstorm and see examples
fully permitted with citation and ability to explain
documents.stance_why: The page tells faculty to 'Develop clear policies for each course' and offers three sample syllabus statements ('not permitted', 'only permitted to help you brainstorm', 'fully permitted, but you must cite the tool') depending on 'whether AI tools will be banned or permitted'. The page itself chooses none, so it delegates with templates.
documents.summary: Archived OTEAR page for Rutgers faculty on AI. It gives advice to learn the tools, redesign assignments and write course policies, three sample syllabus statements, an FAQ on limits and deterrence, and long lists of tools, events and readings that carry little policy content.

units.why: The page frames AI learning as 'shared learning' among students, staff and faculty under 'critical AI literacy'; it is a framing of AI-literacy work, nearest P70 (AI-literacy provision) though it is not a training offer.
units.anchor: a process of shared learning that we think of in terms of critical AI literacy
units.frag_start: Students, staff, and faculty alike are naturally keen
units.fit_note: Framing of critical AI literacy as shared learning, not a training offer.

units.why: Notes chatbots may be 'superficial, inaccurate, biased, or confabulated' and trained on scraped data; a statement of limits and harms, P53.
units.anchor: may be superficial, inaccurate, biased, or “confabulated.”
units.frag_start: Chatbots of this kind work through statistical modeling

units.why: Describes OTEAR providing 'workshops, discussions, and numerous resources' so faculty and staff stay current on AI; support for faculty learning, P63.
units.anchor: helping faculty and staff stay up to date in the ever-evolving world of Artificial Intelligence
units.frag_start: OTEAR is dedicated to helping faculty and staff

units.why: The Council's document includes 'a sample of statements for your syllabi' and advice on academic integrity; a resource offered to instructors, so P63 rather than P09 because nothing is required.
units.anchor: a sample of statements for your syllabi, and a list of resources
units.frag_start: a document which provides a brief history of AI

units.why: Advises faculty to 'Learn what AI tools can and cannot do' and experiment before using or restricting AI; faculty-learning advice before setting policy, P63.
units.anchor: Learn what AI tools can and cannot do by reading up on these tools

units.why: 'Test your assignments by submitting them to ChatGPT' advises instructors to check what AI produces on their own assignments, an assignment-design practice, P35.
units.anchor: Test your assignments by submitting them to ChatGPT and/or other AI tools
units.fit_note: A pre-check of assignments rather than a redesign itself.

units.why: Tells instructors who restrict AI to learn the conduct requirements for charging violations; preparing for enforcement, P36.
units.anchor: Become familiar with the student conduct requirements for charging students with violations
units.frag_start: Become familiar with the student conduct
units.fit_note: Procedural readiness for charging violations, not the classification itself.

units.why: Recommends assignments needing 'higher-order thinking' and personal connection that are 'more difficult for students to answer using AI tools'; redesign around AI, P35.
units.anchor: assignments that require students to use higher-order thinking, connect concepts to specific personal experiences

units.why: Recommends 'project-based learning or staged assignments that begin with work in class'; assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: project-based learning or staged assignments that begin with work in class

units.why: Advises rubrics emphasising 'critical thinking, application of knowledge' rather than summary; grading scheme redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Develop rubrics that emphasize critical thinking, application of knowledge
units.frag_end: rather than the restatement of material or summary.

units.why: 'Develop clear policies for each course' asks instructors to state their own AI rules for the course, P09 (state AI expectations).
units.anchor: Develop clear policies for each course.
units.frag_start: Develop clear policies for each course.

units.why: Suggests starting from the code of conduct, which mandates work be 'created without the aid of impermissible technologies'; ties course policy to existing integrity rules, P36.
units.anchor: all work submitted in a course, academic research, or other activity is the student’s own
units.frag_start: that all work submitted in a course
units.fit_note: Quotes the conduct code as a basis for course policy.

units.why: Recommends repeating course learning goals and how they bear on the decision to ban or permit AI; explaining reasons to students, P66.
units.anchor: repeat the learning goals of the course and how these goals are important
units.frag_start: It is useful to repeat the learning goals

units.why: Tells instructors to add text stating conditions 'depending on whether AI tools will be banned or permitted', so the instructor chooses; P04.
units.anchor: Depending on whether AI tools will be banned or permitted, add text that clearly states
units.frag_start: Depending on whether AI tools will

units.why: Sample statement banning ChatGPT in all stages of writing on any assignment; a prohibit-by-default model text, P01.
units.anchor: not permitted in any stages of the writing process on any assignment.
units.frag_start: Use of AI such as ChatGPT is not
units.fit_note: A sample statement for instructors to adopt, scoped to the writing process.

units.why: Sample statement allowing AI only to brainstorm and see examples, with submitted material the student's own; a narrow permission, P15 (brainstorming).
units.anchor: only permitted to help you brainstorm ideas and see examples.
units.frag_start: Use of AI such as ChatGPT is only permitted
units.frag_end: you submit must be your own.
units.fit_note: Also says all submitted material must be the student's own (P29).

units.why: Sample statement fully permitting AI if the student cites the tool and can explain submitted work; P24 chosen over P02 because the stated conditions are cite and explain.
units.anchor: fully permitted, but you must cite the tool and be able to explain any work
units.frag_start: Use of AI such as ChatGPT is fully permitted
units.fit_note: Also requires ability to explain work (P30) and is a full-permission default (P02).

units.why: 'Schools and departments should discuss these issues as the tools and their use evolve' recommends ongoing discussion of changing policy, P54.
units.anchor: Schools and departments should discuss these issues as the tools and their use evolve.

units.why: Notes generative AI 'hallucinations' and fabricated references that require proofreading before the output is trusted; verify output, P31.
units.anchor: AI tools, such as ChatGPT, frequently fabricate information and invent references

units.why: Encourages faculty to give clear instructions on which tools can be used, how to cite them, to discuss in class, and to remind students of the integrity policy; explaining and discussing rules, P66.
units.anchor: provide clear instructions about which tools and resources can be used
units.fit_note: Bundles instructions, citation guidance, in-class discussion and integrity reminders.

units.why: Suggests requiring students to show stages of their work (outlines, drafts) to discourage AI use; process evidence and assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: require students to show stages of their work, e.g. outlines, rough drafts
units.frag_start: One strategy that can be used to discourage

units.why: Recommends sequencing major assignments in steps ('scaffolding'); assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Major assignments can be designed to be submitted in a sequence of steps

units.why: Suggests project assignments where students 'explain' learning through the product and rubrics scoring critical thinking; understanding check through the product, nearest P34.
units.anchor: produce a specific application with personal insights so that they “explain” their learning
units.frag_start: Projects or assignments that require students
units.frag_end: application of knowledge over summary and review.
units.fit_note: Explanation is built into a product, not a live review or interview.

units.why: Suggests personal reflections on the assignment's value and challenges to deter AI use; reflections as a submission requirement, P26.
units.anchor: students can be required to add personal comments such as reflections
units.frag_end: would do differently once the project was completed.
units.fit_note: Reflections are on the assignment, not on AI use.

units.why: Suggests assignments citing class readings, recent scholarship, or student-collected data that AI databases may lack; assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: cite class readings or discussion, or require that they use recent scholarship
units.frag_start: Instructors can also ask that students

units.why: Suggests research papers requiring citations of specific evidence and quotations with search output; assignment redesign, P35.
units.anchor: Research papers that require citations of specific evidence and quotations
units.frag_end: literature searches that include the search output.

units.why: Suggests presenting findings in multimedia, blog, podcast or e-portfolio formats instead of text; format redesign, P35.
units.anchor: might be shared in a multimedia presentation, blog or podcast, webpage or e-portfolio

units.why: Lists ways AI can be used in college courses (language practice, organizing drafts, self-assessment questions, personalized tutor); possible permitted uses, closest P12 (tutor).
units.anchor: use as personalized tutor for improving learning
units.frag_start: AI can be used in a variety of ways in college courses
units.fit_note: List also covers brainstorming, drafting and self-assessment questions (P14, P15) as examples.

notes: Both documents are university-layer; no school or computing documents. OTEAR page is marked archived/unmaintained and points to the OIT page. Event listings, tool lists, reading lists and navigation were not coded. Topics drawn from the AGENT_BRIEF starter codebook.
